note: Subject–Object–Verb: 'I water drink.' The 을 on 물 is a tag that says 'this is the thing being acted on' — which is why Korean can shuffle words and still make sense.
밥 is literally cooked rice but stands in for food and meals in general — eating 밥 just means eating.
'Like' is a verb here (좋아하다), so it goes to the end like any other verb, and the thing you like takes the object tag 를.
공부하다 is 공부 (studying) + 하다 (do) — 'to do studying.' Every ~하다 verb ends in 해요 in the polite form.
가 marks 친구 as the do-er. 'To' isn't a separate word in front — it's the particle 에 glued onto the back of 학교.
Same frame as going to school — swap the place, keep the skeleton. Korean present tense covers English 'go' and 'am going' both.
있다 means 'to exist' — so this is both 'there's water' and 'I have water.' Korean has no separate everyday verb for having; things just exist (for you).
A structure with no English twin: Korean says 'time not-exists' rather than 'I don't have time.' The owner (me) is simply understood and dropped — Korean omits anything obvious from context.
맛있다 is literally 맛 (taste) + 있다 (exists) — 'taste exists.' Describing words are verbs in Korean, so no 'is' is needed.
The same sentence as 'I drink water' with one swap: 친구가 instead of 저는. The particles do the work; the verb never changes for the subject.
The subject stays first — it's the VERB that moves to the end. And 'to' isn't a separate word in front; it's the particle 에 glued onto the back of 가게 (store).
Same skeleton with a different subject: 가 marks 친구 as the do-er, 를 marks 커피 as the thing liked, verb caps it off.

Four pieces now: subject, then place, then object, then verb. 에서 (not just 에) marks where an action happens — a small preview of Module 2. Typical order is S–Place–O–V, but the particles do the real work.
Same pattern as 'I go to the store' — swap the pieces, keep the skeleton. This is why learning the frame once pays off forever.
Your first past tense: 만나다 → drop 다, last vowel is ㅏ so add 았어요 → 만났어요. The subject is understood and simply dropped.
에 marks time too — 아침에 'in the morning'. 먹다's stem vowel is ㅓ, so the past is 먹었어요.
Actions happen with 에서, not 에 — the cafe is the venue, not the destination. 마시다 → 마셨어요.
The S–Place–O–V frame you previewed in Module 1 (학교에서), now official: 에서 marks where the studying happens.
도 doesn't stack on 을/를 — it replaces it. 음악을도 is wrong; 음악도 carries both 'object' and 'also' at once.
하고 glued to a noun means 'with'. 보다 contracts in the past: 보 + 았어요 → 봤어요.
Destinations keep 에 even in the past. 가다 → 갔어요 — the ㅏ stem and 았 merge into one syllable.
회사 is literally 'company', but 회사에서 일해요 is just 'I'm at work'. 일하다 = 일 (work) + 하다 (do) → 일해요.
The present tense covers the near future — 내일 만나요 needs no 'will'. The time word does the work.
하고 between nouns is 'and' — and only the last noun in the list takes 을/를. 사다 → 샀어요.
듣다 is a ㄷ-irregular: before a vowel ending, ㄷ softens to ㄹ — 들어요, 들었어요. A small family of verbs (걷다 'walk', 묻다 'ask') does the same.
Time-에 once more: 주말에 'on the weekend'. Time words like to lead the sentence, before even the subject.
맵다 → 매워요: the ㅂ softens to 워 before a vowel. A whole family of ㅂ-adjectives does this — file the shape, the full rule comes later.
Negation is one tiny word: 안 sits directly before the verb. No do-support, no word-order gymnastics — 안 먹어요, done.
못 is 안's cousin with a different meaning: not won't — CAN'T. 안 마셔요 is a choice; 못 마셔요 is ability or circumstance.
Wanting bolts onto the verb stem: 먹다 → 먹고 싶어요. Any verb works — drop 다, add 고 싶어요.
The Module 2 pattern with the new meal word: time-에 up front, past tense at the end.
Everything recycled from Module 2 in one breath: action-place 에서, noun-joining 하고, past 샀어요.
만들다 → 만들었어요. The S–O–V skeleton hasn't changed since your first sentence — only the bricks get richer.
-고 싶어요 again with a new verb: 시키다 → 시키고 싶어요. 시키다 is the everyday word for ordering in.
The 없어요 pattern from Module 1, mid-recipe: 'sugar not-exists' = we're out of sugar.
Describing words are verbs, so tastes conjugate like actions: 짜다 → 짜요, 달다 → 달아요.
배고프다 → 배고파요: the ㅡ drops before 아. You met this sentence's soul in the gap deck — 'stomach is hungry.'
싫어하다 is 좋아하다's opposite and works identically: the disliked thing takes 을/를, the verb caps the sentence.
Module 2's 식당 finally gets its sentence. 주문하다 is the proper restaurant word; 시키다 is its casual twin.
One word, whole sentence — subject understood, 배부르다 → 배불러요 (a 르-irregular; just bank this form). The natural end of any good meal.
우리 가족 — 'our family' even when you mean yours alone. And 살다 takes 에, not 에서: where you live is where you exist, not where you act.
The copula glues onto the noun itself: 선생님 + 이에요. After a consonant it's 이에요; after a vowel, 예요.
The same sentence one register up: 입니다 is the 합니다-style copula. Say it in interviews and introductions; say 학생이에요 everywhere else.
The -(으)시- honorific hides inside 오세요 (오 + 시 + 어요). It elevates the SUBJECT — you use it about respected people, never about yourself.
Honorifics don't just add 시 — some verbs get replaced outright. Elders don't 먹다; they 드시다.
-(으)시- works on describing words too: 바쁘다 → 바쁘세요. Your own parents get honorifics when you talk about them.
Not-knowing is its own verb — 모르다, not 안 알다. 르-irregular: 몰라요, like 배불러요.
A Module 2 sentence promoted to the 합니다 style: 일해요 → 일합니다. Same meaning, more starch — this is self-introduction register.
가수 ends in a vowel, so the copula is 예요 (not 이에요). And 오빠 tells you the speaker is female — sibling words carry the speaker's gender.
Inside the family, casual words and plain 해요체 are normal — 아빠 cooks; 아버지 would 요리하세요 in front of guests.
반말, mechanically: 가요 minus the 요. That's the whole trick — but only with close friends, younger family, or kids.
Another vowel-final noun, another 예요. 언니 marks the speaker as female — a male speaker would say 누나는 의사예요.
Module 2's 하고-'with' at the family table. 밥을 먹다 is such a unit that it rides in the verb chunk here — eating rice is just eating.
있다's honorific replacement: respected people don't 있다, they 계시다. With 우리 집 — 'our house' — doing its warm Korean thing.
몇 + counter is the question machine: 몇 시 (what hour), 몇 명 (how many people), 몇 살 (how old). The copula rides on the counter.
The hybrid clock in one sentence: hours take native numbers (세 시), minutes take Sino (십 분). Every Korean clock-reading mixes both systems.
반 (half) replaces 삼십 분 the way 'half past' replaces 'thirty' — and 오전/오후 go BEFORE the time, not after.
The counting frame: [thing] [number] [counter] — 커피 두 잔, never 두 커피. The object particle usually drops off counted phrases in speech.
Age = native number + 살 + copula. 열 keeps its full form — only 하나/둘/셋/넷/스물 contract before counters.
A normal early question in Korea — age decides speech register (Module 4!), so it's practical, not rude. To an elder, upgrade the noun: 연세가 어떻게 되세요?
How Koreans state family size: 'our family is four people.' 넷 contracts to 네 before the people-counter 명.
마리 counts animals — including the ones you're about to cook. Two fish at the market: 생선 두 마리.
Same counting frame inside a full Module 2 past-tense sentence. The pieces keep composing — that's the whole course thesis.
읽다 finally in action: 읽었어요 — the buried ㄹ surfaces (il-geo-sseo-yo). 셋 → 세 before the counter.
Days take time-에 like 아침 and 주말 did. Two 에s in one sentence, doing two jobs — time and destination.
Module 4's copula welding two Module 5 nouns. 금요일 + 이에요 — the day itself takes no particle here.
The 있어요-have pattern from Module 1: plans exist (for me). 약속 있어요 is the standard 'I've got plans' — see the gap deck for why it's not a solemn vow.
하나 → 한 before its counter, the most common contraction of all: 한 잔, 한 명, 한 개. 매일 needs no particle — it's self-sufficiently adverbial.
The single most useful sentence in this course. 어디 sits exactly where the answer will: 화장실이 [어디]에 있어요? → [저기]에 있어요.
The location frame: [thing]은/는 [landmark] [position]에 있어요. Position words are NOUNS — 병원 옆 is literally 'the hospital's side.'
Position 안 (inside) after the noun — not to be confused with negation 안, which stands before a verb. Same sound, opposite neighborhoods.
'On' = 위에, 'the desk's topside-at.' English prepositions come BEFORE; Korean position nouns come AFTER, then 에 seals the phrase.
(으)로 marks a HEADING, not a destination — 왼쪽으로 is 'leftward.' Compare 학교에 가요 (to school, the endpoint) with 학교로 가요 (in the school's direction).
(으)로's second job: means. 지하철로 = by subway. After ㄹ it's bare 로 — 지하철로, not 지하철으로.

note: The time bracket: 부터 opens it, 까지 closes it. Everything inside is Module 5 — the course is compounding.
The space bracket: 에서 opens it (from), 까지 closes it (as far as). And 걷다 is a ㄷ-irregular like 듣다: 걸어요.
There-is and location are one pattern in Korean: 'park exists at house's front' covers both 'there's a park in front' and 'the park is in front.'
Same frame, new position noun. Swap 옆/앞/뒤/위/아래 in and out — the skeleton never moves.
가깝다 → 가까워요, the same ㅂ-softening as 맵다 → 매워요. Its partner 멀다 stays regular: 멀어요.
The magic taxi words. Getting off happens FROM a place, so 여기 takes 에서 — the action-location particle earning its keep.

en.t: between the bank and the supermarket

note: 사이 (the between-space) is a noun like every position word: A하고 B 사이에 = 'at A-and-B's between.'
What you ride is a direct object in Korean: 버스를 타요, 'ride the bus.' Compare 지하철로 가요, where the subway is the means, not the thing acted on.
The load-bearing wall of small talk. Any 하다-adjective conjugates like the verb: 따뜻하다 → 따뜻해요.
-지만 welds 'but' onto the first verb: drop 다, add 지만. Only the final verb carries the politeness 요 — the welded one travels light.
Connectives open the NEXT sentence: cause, full stop, 그래서, result. Your first two-sentence unit — this is what talking actually sounds like.
Division of labor: 하고 joins nouns inside a sentence; 그리고 joins whole sentences. With Module 2's 도 tagging along.
The truest sentence in this course. 그런데 is the soft pivot; 어렵다 goes ㅂ-irregular: 어려워요.
-지만 on a Module 4 adjective, no subject needed. Note 바쁘지만 keeps the ㅡ — the drop only happens before 아/어, and 지만 starts with ㅈ.
Colors are nouns ([hue] + 색), so they take the copula: 빨간색이에요, 'is red-color.' The Module 4 machine keeps paying rent.
Module 1's 예쁘다 returns with its ㅡ-drop showing: 예뻐요. The 슬프다/바쁘다/배고프다 family keeps growing.
Subject and object both understood — context carries everything, the verb carries the feeling. The most famous dropped-subject sentence in Korean.
Feelings are stated body-outward, like 배고프다: not 'I feel good' but 'the mood is good.' The self is implied, the state is the subject.
The ㅡ-drop in the past: 슬프다 → 슬펐어요. Both sentences in past tense — Korean keeps the timeline consistent across the 그래서.
하지만 is the firm 'but' — a real contrast follows. 듣다's ㄷ-irregular from Module 2 rides again: 들어요.
The Swiss-army sentence. As a question: are you okay? As an answer: I'm fine — or no thanks. The gap deck sorts out its three jobs.
Module 1's 시간이 없어요, answered at last. 많다 → 많아요, the ㅎ falling silent — abundance stated the same exist-style way as lack.
Clock times take 에, like every time expression — and it's the native number before 시, exactly as Module 5 drilled.
No 'my' needed — whose hands would they be? Korean drops possessives the way it drops subjects: anything obvious goes unsaid.
Meet 이 the tooth — same syllable as 이 (two) and the subject particle. The gap deck throws a small party for this overworked sound.
The progressive: verb stem + 고 있어요. 있다 moonlights again — this time as 'be in the middle of.' The classic phone answer to 뭐 해요?
No 'for' — what you await is a plain direct object: 친구를 기다려요. English prepositions keep dissolving into Korean particles.
The future: stem + -(으)ㄹ 거예요. 쉬다 ends in a vowel, so the ㄹ hooks straight on: 쉴 거예요. Resting is an action, so home takes 에서.
Every 하다 verb futures the same way: 하다 → 할 거예요. And 방 finally enters the vocabulary — Father can now enter the room officially.
Consonant stems take the full 을: 먹을 거예요. Both futures in one pattern — ㄹ after vowels, 을 after consonants, 거예요 always.

note: 오늘은 — the topic particle marking a CONTRAST: 'as for today (unlike usual).' 은/는's second job, quietly doing what English does with stress.
The frequency ladder slots in before the place and verb: 항상 (always) > 보통 (usually) > 자주 (often) > 가끔 (sometimes).
끝나다 — the thing ends by itself, no one ending it. And 여덟 시 puts Module 5's trickiest number straight to work.
Nouns stack directly: 주말 계획, 'weekend plans.' The 있어요-have pattern asks the Friday-afternoon question of every office.
Adjectives take the future too — 바쁠 거예요. On adjectives and other people it shades toward 'probably': the gap deck covers the blur.
하다 as 'to play' — games, like studying and work, are things you DO. Module 1's do-everything verb keeps collecting jobs.
The most useful conjugation in Korean: 주다 + 세요. [Anything] 주세요 and the thing arrives. Particles usually drop off — the frame is that strong.
Module 5's counting frame docks straight into 주세요: [thing] [number] [counter] 주세요. This one pattern orders everything in Korea.
얼마 + the copula — a complete shopping toolkit in three syllables. Point at anything and deploy.
Prices are SINO territory: 오천 원. Module 2's numbers grow their big siblings — 백, 천, 만 — and suddenly you can read every price tag.
-(으)세요's second job: a polite request TO you (Module 4 used it as a statement ABOUT elders — same ending, context decides; the gap deck sorts it).
The emergency word. 주다 inside a verb means 'do it FOR me' — help-give. One word, complete sentence, genuinely worth memorizing today.
The do-for-me machine generalizes: [verb]-아/어 주세요. 보여 주세요, 바꿔 주세요, 말해 주세요 — request anything done on your behalf.
포장 (wrapping) + 하다 + 주세요 — the takeout sentence. Watch cafes transform at the sound of it.
-(으)ㄹ까요? floats a proposal: shall we? And 같이 hides a sound rule — it's pronounced 가치, exactly the interlude's ㅌ+이 story.
-(으)ㅂ시다 — 'let's' with a bit of starch (rally-the-team energy). Among friends, plain 같이 가요 does the same job more softly.
더 slots anywhere quantity lives: 더 주세요 (more please), and — at the table where 반찬 refills are free — the politest two words you know.
받다 — 주다's other half. Korean social life runs on the give-receive axis, and now you own both verbs.
What every cashier asks: 봉투 드릴까요? (bag?), 영수증 드릴까요? (receipt?). 드리다 is humble giving — they give upward, to you, the honored 손님.
The classic rainy-day transaction, in the frame you've owned since Module 2. Nothing new here — which is the point. It's all composition now.
Ability is existence: [verb]-(으)ㄹ 수 있다 = 'a way-to-[verb] exists.' The 있다 factory's grandest product — the gap deck has the blueprint.
Speaking a language is DOING it: 한국어를 해요. Ten modules in, this sentence is now simply true — say it to the next Korean speaker you meet.
-(으)ㄹ 수 없어요 is the formal negative; Module 3's 못 is its everyday shortcut — 운전 못 해요 means the same, faster.

-아/어서 welds cause to result: late-so-sorry. THE apology formula — Module 8's 늦다 meets Module 4's 죄송합니다, and you will use this sentence.
The because-pair's division of labor: before a request or command, use -(으)니까 — never -아/어서. Statements take either; imperatives are 니까 territory.
The learner's shield. Its twin: 다시 말해 주세요 (again, please). Deploy both freely — Koreans respond with warmth, not impatience.
Past tense as 'done-ness': the understanding either happened or it didn't. Honest answer available: 이해 못 했어요.
무슨 sits before its noun: what-kind-of meaning? Point at any word, deploy, learn. (M5's 무슨 요일이에요? IOU: paid.)

덥다 → 더워요: the ㅂ-irregular family's flagship, finally formalized. Korean summers earn the 아주.
춥다 → 추워요, same ㅂ→우 move. 너무 officially means 'excessively' but colloquially it's just 'so' — Koreans 너무 everything.

Seasons take time-에 like every time word. Two blossom weeks a year, and this sentence gets a nation outdoors.
The national autumn pilgrimage — 단풍 season. Korea is 70% 산; hiking gear is practically a uniform.
Module 10's can-machine, one week old, already composing with new vocabulary. This is Band 2's whole deal: new fuel, same engine.
타다 rides everything: buses, bikes, and now skis. One verb, an entire transport-and-sports vocabulary unlocked.
눈 + 사람 — a compound you could have decoded in Module 1. The dropped subject covers 'I' and 'we' alike; snow days imply company.
Module 10's rule, obeyed: a proposal follows, so the reason takes -(으)니까. Three modules of glue in eight syllables.

Module 12's -(으)러 가다 with fresh cargo. House-hunting is mostly this sentence plus 몇 층이에요?.

The don't-machine: stem + -지 마세요, no sound rules, no exceptions. This is its most-said sentence in the language.
The symptom template: [body part]가 아파요. Swap M2's 도 in when the list grows — and with 아프다 the ㅡ-drop patriarch is finally official.
M12's 걸리다 with its other job: to be caught. A cold catches YOU in Korean — 감기에 걸리다, caught on the illness like a coat on a hook.
Korean EATS medicine — 약을 먹다, no swallowing verb needed. M13's -(으)ㄴ 후에 sequences the doctor's orders; 푹 makes the rest thorough.
M13's -기 전에 carrying M8's tooth-이 and 닦다 — same blocks, never the same sentence. The 이 syllable's fourth job stays employed.
A fever 'exists' — the 있다-factory does diagnostics. And 병원 finally decomposes: 병 (illness) + 원 (house), the illness-house.
-지 마세요 on a full sentence frame — place, object, prohibition. Read it off every wall in Korea as 금연.
The examination-table sentence. ㅂ-irregular 눕다 goes 누우- before -(으)세요 — the 더워요 rule, now taking requests.
-지 마세요 attaches to adjectives too — M8's 늦다 takes the prohibition. M8's contrast-은 hints today matters more than usual.
Stress is 'received' in Korean — M9's 받다 promoted to psychology — and energy 'doesn't exist.' Two structural gaps in one diagnosis.
THE get-well-soon. 낫다 opens Korean's rarest irregular family: the ㅅ vanishes before vowels — 나으세요, 나아요. M12's 빨리 sets the tempo.
M13's -(으)ㄴ 후에 on a 하다-verb: 운동하다 → 운동한. Module 1's very first noun, still hydrating.

rom: nuni apayo. geuraeseo iljjik jal geoyeyo
note: 눈이 아파요 — the eye, not the snow; the homograph earns its keep. M7's 그래서 chains into M8's future, and 자다 contracts: 잘 거예요.
Korean reports illness through the body: 'my body isn't good.' No 'I feel' verb required — M3's 안 does the softening.
The -기 from M13's 자기 전에, new machine: [verb]-기 + 시작하다 = start to. Also: this sentence is true of you, which feels good to say.
M11's rain-comes riding the new machine — the moment 장마 season announces itself. Weather verbs love -기 시작하다.
M14's don't-machine, first day at school. Given the 학원 schedule (vocab note), Korean teachers say this with real sympathy.
잊다 sounds exactly like 있다 — but 잊지 마세요 vs 있지요 can't be confused in context. M10's 숙제 finally gets assigned.
M5's 몇 counting school years, M4's copula asking. Spelled 학년, said 항년 — the interlude's nasalization rule grading papers.
M13's noun-전에 on M10's exam, and 외우다 doing what this app is named for — 단어, one word at a time.
The classroom's two verbs meet: 선생님이 가르쳐요, 학생이 배워요. M4's teacher finally teaching.
Questions 'exist' before they're asked — the 있다-factory again. 물어보다 = ask-and-see; the 보다 makes the asking gentler.
The app's own feedback loop, spoken aloud. M10's 다시 — again — is how anything gets learned.
Korean SEES exams — 시험을 보다 (gap deck). So doing well is seeing one well: 잘 봤어요. M1's 보다 picks up its strangest job.
M7's -지만 with M7's ㅂ-irregular 어렵다 — 어렵지만 keeps its ㅂ because no vowel follows. Say it about any subject; the structure forgives.
The eternal resolution: M6's 부터 sets the start line, M8's future makes the promise, -기 시작하다 does the starting. Tomorrow.
M14's symptom machinery excusing you from M2's 읽다 — same blocks as last module, never the same sentence. 읽어요 says 일거요; the interlude explains.
M6's (으)로 in its tool job — write BY MEANS OF pencil. Exam instructions in four syllables.
The try-machine: verb-아/어 + 보다 — do it AND SEE. M15 taught 보다 to watch exams; now it watches attempts. Every Korean host says this sentence.
M6's (으)로 marking the tool — the tool is the language. The try-flavor is what makes it kind: no stakes, just see how it goes.
M15's 외우다 through the try-machine, carrying M13's 새 — the app's daily request, now in the app's own language.
다니다 — the enrolled-going verb. 가다 is one trip; 다니다 says the place expects you back. Works for 학교, 학원, 교회, gyms you pay for and visit twice.
M5's native-number clock scheduling the day's sweetest verb. The 근-family tells the whole workday: 출근, 퇴근, 야근.
M10's -아/어서 filing the honest report. The gap deck's 월화수목금금금 explains the schedule that makes this sentence so common.
M14's don't-machine meets the office's sternest verb — 지각 is lateness as an official offense, not just M8's casual 늦다.
M6's (으)로 in its by-means-of job again — pencil, language, email; the particle doesn't care what the tool is.
M15's start-machine on M2's oldest verb — first job energy. Family news travels in exactly this sentence shape.
M15's 틀리다 is wrong answers; 실수 is wrong actions — and M7's 괜찮아요 still absorbs both. The healthiest sentence in the module.
쓰다's job collection grows again: write (연필로 쓰세요), use, and now spend. One ㅡ-drop verb, three careers. The sentence is also just true.
M14's don't-machine, M15's textbook, this module's copier — three modules, one copyright notice.
이번 + 달: this-turn's month. M4's ㅡ-drop 바쁘다 doing what it does most — 바빠요, said with a sigh.

끝나다 — it ended by itself (compare 끝내다, where you end it). M11's 휴가 as the reward, with contrast-은 marking the turn: NOW, vacation. Fun fact: the first draft of this sentence was rejected by the app's own no-repeats validator — 다음 주부터 휴가예요 already exists in Module 11.
The small-talk trinity's third question, after job and age. Your answer machine is this module's glue — read on.
The nominalizer, deployed: 요리하다 → 요리하는 것 — 'the cooking thing' — and suddenly a verb can be liked, owned, discussed. This is the single most useful pattern left in Korean.
The full answer to 취미가 뭐예요?: [verb]-는 것 + the M4 copula. 제 — the humble 'my' matching 저 — finally arrives to claim the hobby.
The nominalizer feeding M8's progressive — two machines chained. 있다's job count stopped being news modules ago.
보다's original job, for once — actually watching. 축구 경기 stacks noun-on-noun, no particle needed between them.
Contrast-은 on both days, M7's -지만 as the hinge — the win/lose pair in one sports recap. Every fan's Tuesday.
M16's 회식 flowing into the 노래방 through M13's 후에 — the standard trajectory of a Korean work evening, and three modules in one sentence.
M16's try-machine handing you an instrument. 치다 + 어 → 쳐 — the same squeeze as 가르쳐요.

en.t: I play the piano well, but

note: 잘 치다 vs 못하다 — the good-at/bad-at pair in one honest self-assessment. The gap deck's 음치 has a word for the second half.
M4's warm 우리 doing what it does best. Red shirts, drums, the whole city in the square — 응원 is a team sport itself.
많이 — the overdue adverb of abundance, said 마니 — finally official. M11's 산 hosting the national 등산-and-photograph ritual.
별로 + M3's 안 — the double-softened dislike. The nominalizer makes even avoidance grammatical. A deeply honest sentence.
매주 extends M5's 매일 across the calendar. 산책's 산 is a stroll, not M11's summit — the homograph radar catches another one.
Popularity is POSSESSED in Korean — 인기가 많아요, 'has much popularity' — the 있다-chassis one more time. Objectively true sentence.

en.t: I will eat well (said before eating)

note: The before-eating formula — thanks to whoever cooked or paid. Inside it, a preview: -겠- marks intention ('I WILL eat well'). Memorize the whole thing; the grammar comes free.
The after-eating bookend — and a minimal pair with 먹겠습니다: swap -겠- (will) for -었- (did) and intention becomes gratitude. Two formulas, one grammar lesson hiding in plain sight.
The menu-panic escape hatch: M10's 뭐 asks, M9's do-for-me machine requests. Servers take this question seriously — expect a real answer.
M17's match flowing into M3's 시키다 through M13's 후에 — the 치맥 supply chain. On big match nights, delivery apps genuinely buckle.
굽다 joins the ㅂ-irregular verbs: 구워요. Table-grill culture: tongs get passed, the youngest flips, everyone claims they're full and keeps eating.
M17's nominalizer meets M16's 중요하다 — and the dish meets its own verb: 비빔밥 is 비비다's noun wearing 밥. Mix it all the way down; half-mixed is half-lived.
The midnight national anthem. M3's 배고프다 through M10's -아서, resolving in 끓이다 — you boil it, it doesn't boil itself (the agency split from 끝나다/끝내다).
The street-food thesis statement — M7's -지만 weld, M3's 맵다 keeping its ㅂ before the consonant. The pain is part of the price.
Every 찌개 arrives with this warning, and it is always true. 뜨겁다 (hot to touch) vs M11's 덥다 (hot weather) — English merges them, Korean won't.
M3's 반찬 arrive unordered, unlimited, and refillable — 반찬 더 주세요 works with M9's 더. The table fills before the meal even starts.
Said with the confidence of someone who waited forty minutes to prove it. M6's 여기 + the taste-house — the sentence every food pilgrimage ends on.
외식 — outside-eating — as a household holiday. M9's 같이 (said 가치, per the interlude) makes it an invitation.
Literally 'dry the glass.' Etiquette rides along: juniors clink lower and turn slightly away to drink — M4's politeness ladder, operating at the table.
M17's nominalizer wearing M2's 도, absorbed by M7's all-purpose 괜찮아요. The gap deck's 혼밥 has made solo dining a named, normal thing — this sentence is its motto.
M4's bare 안녕 finally gets its module — and 이야 is the casual copula, 이에요 with the formality snapped off. Welcome to 반말.
The most-sent text message in Korea. Questions in 반말 need no machinery at all — drop the 요, raise the pitch, done.
-자: the let's-ending, 반말's own propositive — M9's -(으)ㅂ시다 with the tie loosened. M12's -(으)러 rides along; M18's 떡볶이 is the destination.
반말 drops particles too — no 가 after 여기, casual speech travels light. M11's 진짜 is the native intensity setting for this register.
와! — a whole command in one syllable: 오다 conjugated to 와요, minus the 요. Casual commands are just the -아/어 form, bare.
Said 추카해 — the ㅎ-merge the sound interlude promised. Add -요 for politeness, 합니다 for ceremony; the song uses this exact casual form.
M4's register ladder in action: 죄송합니다 → 미안해요 → 미안해. And 화나다 — anger COMES OUT, weather-style, like 비가 와요. Feelings arrive on their own in Korean.
아니다 — the negative copula you've conjugated since M4's 아니에요 — in its casual skin. 괜찮아, minus its 요, still absorbs everything.
너 — the 'you' Korean spends most of its energy avoiding — is safe here, between friends. 최고야: highest praise, lowest register.
M7's 웃다 as a bare casual command: 웃어! The full escalation available: 웃으세요 (please laugh) → 웃어 (laugh!) → silence (the joke failed).
M14's -지 마세요 loses its 세요 and becomes -지 마 — the casual prohibition. Same machine, shorter lever. Often really means 'no WAY!'
놀다 — play as a kid, hang out as an adult, no embarrassment either way. 놀자 is the friendship imperative; the ㄹ stays put before -자.
The sentence that starts every rumor. -지 마 again — in 반말, prohibitions come in two syllables and are ignored in one.
Module 18 said 오늘 같이 외식해요; a friend says 외식하자 — same happy plan, register swapped. That shift IS this module.
여보세요 — phone-only, never face to face. M10's 누구 wearing M9's -세요: the politest possible 'who ARE you.'
-(으)면: the if/when hinge. Consonant stems take 으면 (있으면), vowel stems take 면 — the vowel-checking habit you've had since -(으)세요.
M4's 모르다 straight into the new hinge — 르-verbs keep their dictionary shape before -면. M16's try-machine finishes the advice. The whole modern epistemology in five syllables.
M11's weather-comes through the conditional into M8's future — three modules, one lazy Sunday plan.
The modern alibi, fully machined: batteries 'don't exist' when dead, M10's -어서 files the excuse, M3's 못 confirms the incapacity.
잃다 + M13's 버리다 as the oops-completely auxiliary: lost AND gone. The modern nightmare in one verb; Korea's lost-and-found culture is your best hope — phones actually come back.
전화 + 번호, self-assembling. Korean numbers recite digit by digit with M2's Sino set — 공일공 (010) opens nearly all of them.
Pure M19 반말 — particles dropped, 요 gone, urgency intact. The gap deck's 읽씹 is what this sentence is fighting against.

en.t: I posted it on social media

note: M17's 찍다 aims at yourself, then 올리다 LIFTS the result onto the internet — Korean uploads by raising. The 인증샷 culture (gap deck) explains the why.
M19's 연락하다 through the hinge into M10's can-machine — 놀다 keeps its ㄹ before -(으)ㄹ 수: 놀 수. An open invitation, fully grammatical.
M19's 비밀 + 번호 = a secret-number, promptly forgotten with M15's 잊다. Intensify honestly with 잊어버렸어요 — forgot-and-gone, like 잃어버리다.
True of nearly every café in the country. Follow-up you can now build yourself: 비밀번호가 뭐예요?

en.t: If I turn off the alarm,

note: M13's 끄다 before -면 keeps its ㅡ (the drop only happens before 아/어). A conditional stating a law of nature.
The hinge composes: -(으)면 + M10's 안 돼요 = 'if you press it, not okay' — Korean's standard must-not. You've unlocked a whole family of warnings for free.
The looks-machine: -아/어 + 보이다 — it APPEARS stylish. 보다's fourth career (see, watch-exams, try, and now seem). Deploy generously; it costs nothing.
The looks-machine as care: noticing counts as kindness in Korean, and this pair is how it's said. M16's 야근 usually explains the answer.
In age-calibrated Korea (M19's gap deck), looking younger than your years is elite news — this might be the country's most reliable compliment. Accept with 아니에요 and visible delight.
M16's try-machine in the fitting room — wear-and-see. The shopkeeper's invitation; the 탈의실 (changing room) is where it leads.
에 + 는 stack — in-winter, as-for: particles compound like Lego. M8's 입다 covers the torso; the wear-verb table covers the rest of you.
M12's 편하다 — comfortable — migrating from subway seats to denim. Blue-pants: the compound tells you the color.
M20's hinge on its 'when' setting, M6's (으)로 marking the destination outfit, and 갈아입다 — M12's 갈아타다 transferring between clothes instead of trains.
The shop's second-favorite sentence, and — unlike some of its favorites — often true. Also said of couples and food pairings: harmony is harmony.
M9's softener 좀 + the price-cutting verb through the do-for-me machine. Live ammunition at 시장 stalls; a warm smile at department stores. Know your venue.
M20's hinge + M3's 안 + M8's future: a budget, fully grammaticalized. 사다 keeps its ㄹ-future shape: 살 거예요.
Korea-clothes, per the compound. M1's ㅡ-drop 예쁘다 doing what it was born for. Rent one near a palace and admission is free — the deal of the tourism century.
M15's 맞다 — right answers then, right fit now: correctness and fitting share a verb in Korean. The fitting room's most common verdict.
The -복 suffix at work: 교복, 수영복, 한복 — one syllable clothes entire contexts. M15's school system, now in uniform.
M20's internet meets M20's hinge meets M7's 싸다 — the sentence behind Korea's overflowing delivery lobbies. 사면/싸요: one tense vowel apart; the confusables drill trained you for this.
The comparison machine: [loser]보다 더 [adjective]. That 보다 is a PARTICLE wearing the verb's spelling — the syllable's fifth job. M9's 더 finally reveals its grammar career.
M12's transit rivalry, finally adjudicated by grammar. 빠르다's 르-conjugation (빨라요) has been yours since the last train.
제일 — literally 'number one' (M2's Sino 일!) — parks before any adjective and crowns it. 아름답다 goes ㅂ-irregular for the occasion: 아름다워요.

rom: yeoreum otboda gyeoul oseul deo joahaeyo
note: The comparison machine handles preferences too — [rejected]보다 [chosen]을 더 좋아해요. M11's seasons and M21's closet, ranked.
The 한강 lifestyle (gap deck): delivery scooters find your picnic blanket by GPS. M3's 치킨 has now appeared at the match, the 회식, and the river — the true main character.
야경 = night-야 + scenery-경 — and yes, that's the third 야 the radar has logged (night, field, and this compound's night again). M17's 유명하다 confirms what the postcards claim.
The interlude's promised 고양이 arrives — batchim ㅇ staying seated, as advertised — and immediately wins an argument with M13's 조용하다.
피다 — the verb M14's 피우다 (make-bloom → smoke) was built on. Korea forecasts the 벚꽃 front like weather, city by city, to the day. The gap deck's 꽃구경 is the pilgrimage.

rom: sigoreun gonggiga joayo. geureonde jogeum simsimhaeyo
note: The urban Korean's honest review of the countryside, M7's 그런데 hinging the trade-off. 공기가 좋아요 — air quality as compliment; M11's 미세먼지 made it one.
M21's looks-machine on M11's sky — and a real Korean saying: autumn is when 'the sky is high and horses fatten' (천고마비). The clear air genuinely does it.
M20's hinge, M21's shoes and foot-verb, M11's mountain — though be warned: actual Korean hikers will outdress you in full alpine gear for a hill with a coffee shop on top.
M4's 우리 claiming the neighborhood, M12's 편하다 measuring it, 제일 crowning it. Everyone's 동네 wins this contest; that's what 동네 means.

rom: uri eomma yoriga sesangeseo jeil masisseoyo
note: 세상에서 제일 — the superlative's biggest stage. 우리 엄마, per M4's rule, even when she's only yours. A sentence that is grammatically superlative and factually correct in every household.
M11's 그치다 through M13's 후에, resolved by plain old seeing — 보다's first job, for the prettiest payoff. Three bands of the course in one sky.
-(으)면 돼요: 'if you do X, it's fine' = JUST do X. M20 gave you the must-not (누르면 안 돼요); flip the polarity and directions become this easy.
M9's attention-getter opens, M6's 어디 asks, the 있다-frame locates. 박물관 says 방물관 — the interlude's nasalization, museum edition.
M6's 왼쪽 was a 쪽-compound all along — this module hands over the raw 쪽. Directions in Korea come as chains of exactly this sentence.
Four syllables that decide whether you walk or wave down a taxi. M6's 멀다 keeps its ㄹ: 멀어요.

rom: du sigan jeone gonghange dochakhamyeon dwaeyo
note: M5's counted hours through M13's 전에 into the it's-fine machine — three modules of glue delivering one piece of airport advice.
M14's don't-machine guarding M15's forget-verb at the front door. The one item with no workaround — everything else, 공항에서 사면 돼요.
M13's 짐 meets M21's 무겁다 — the eternal packing verdict. Said at check-in counters worldwide, one kilo over.
M22's 제일 ranking M12's second city. 바닷가 — the sea's edge — is M11's 바다 grown a shoreline.
M22's leisure-looking applied to six hundred years of architecture. Arrive in M21's 한복 and 경복궁 waives the ticket — the course's best-dressed discount.
M12's purpose-러 on a shopping mission. 기념품 = memory-goods; M3's 시장 is where they're cheapest and 깎아 주세요 still works.
You lose the ROAD in Korean — M20's lost-and-gone verb applied to M12's 길. The 길치 of M17's gap deck says this often, cheerfully.
M22's comparison machine doing trip math with M12's tickets — 표 gluing onto its vehicle exactly as promised back then. The KTX (gap deck) is why the train usually wins.

rom: yeohaeng hue jibe oraomyeon jeil joayo
note: M13's 후에, M20's hinge, M22's 제일 — and the gap deck's 집 떠나면 고생이다 proverb, proven again. Every journey's real destination.
Literally 'almost all came' — arrival measured by the coming already done. The sentence every backseat wants and every driver stretches.
The IOU from M10's 생각하다 note, paid in full: 좋다 wears the badge and parks in front of the noun. 좋은 said 조은 — the ㅎ vanishing per the sound interlude.
A verb clause parked before a noun: 자주 가는 카페 — 'the often-go cafe.' No 'that I' anywhere; the -는 badge IS the relative pronoun.
A whole clause — subject, M22's 제일, verb — wearing one badge. Introductions to songs, foods, and people all run on this shape.
The module's power move: 마음이 착한 — 'heart-is-kind' — a full subject-verb clause turned adjective. Korean has no who/that/which; the badge does it all. M19's 마음 meets M19's 최고.
M23's tourists meet the badge: 관광객이 많은 곳 — 'a tourists-are-many place.' 곳's own M12 note promised this parse; delivered.
The past badge on M9's 사다: 산 — one syllable carrying a whole backstory. (Not the mountain 산 — the homograph radar stays on.) M23's memory-goods, modified.
M23's just-do-X machine at double -면: if-you-don't-know, ask-and-it's-fine. The learner's licence, notarized. 혹시 몰라서 — just in case — is its cousin.
그런 — 그렇다 with the badge — meets M14's -지 마세요. And M7's 그런데 stands revealed: 그런 + 데, 'that kind of situation, and…'
The double-subject trick: as-for-us, thoughts-are-identical. 똑 — the 'exactly' of M23's 똑바로 and the knock of M15's 똑똑하다 — bolted onto 같다.
사실 topic-marked shifts into confession gear. 달라요 is 다르다 in 르-family dress — the 몰라요/빨라요/불러요 shape gains its most-argued member.
어떤 — 어떻다 wearing the badge — asks for a KIND, not a name. 들어요: M2's ㄷ-irregular, still flipping after 22 modules.
The politest way to raise a hand: a curious thing exists. New badge + M17's 것 + the 있다-chassis — every part already owned.
Two exhibits in one: 본 (the past badge on M1's 보다) and 어땠어요 (어떻다 in past tense). Casual speech drops the particle after 영화 — questions move fast.
The national why-deflector, straight from the gap deck's oldest resident: sometimes there is no reason, and Korean has one word for saying so politely.
